1.pericope_label: It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom an hundred and twenty princes, which should be over the whole kingdom; And over these three presidents; of whom Daniel was first: that the princes might give accounts unto them, and the king should have no damage
debates: How many provinces the empire held
Whether the king was to be spared loss or trouble
Why a conqueror promoted a captive of the kingdom he had taken
outliers: Calvin sets aside the received rendering of the purpose clause on lexical grounds, taking it of loss suffered rather than trouble avoided
Keil and Delitzsch alone raise the modern objection that the arrangement described here cannot be reconciled with the number of satraps reported by Xenophon
themes: A conquered kingdom divided into districts overnight
Accounts passing upward through too many hands
An old captive clothed in royal apparel
A crown that gains nothing but more country to watch

3.pericope_label: Then this Daniel was preferred above the presidents and princes, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm. Then the presidents and princes sought to find occasion against Daniel concerning the kingdom; but they could find none occasion nor fault
debates: What being preferred above the rest amounts to
Where the enmity of the officers came from
Why the accusers had to leave the administration and turn to religion
outliers: Calvin leaves the narrative to complain of the kings of his own day, who despise the gifts of God in able men and keep the ignorant about them
Ellicott states the conspiracy as a deliberate engineering of a clash between civil and religious duty, where the others speak only of envy and pretext
themes: Accounts examined too closely for comfort
A man watched by those who cannot fault him
Innocence held up like a shield
A crime that has to be manufactured out of prayer

6.pericope_label: Then these presidents and princes assembled together to the king, and said thus unto him, King Darius, live for ever. All the presidents of the kingdom, the governors, and the princes, the counsellors, and the captains, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a firm decree
debates: Whether the decree had the consent it claimed
What the thirty days were meant to accomplish
Why the king put his name to it
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch argue from the construction that the officers named are all four classes of prefects, not the three presidents, against the reading everyone else assumes
Calvin canvasses two explanations of the motive of Darius and rejects both as insufficient before offering a third
themes: A deputation that arrives shouting
A vote reported as unanimous by two men
A month in which no one may ask anything of heaven
A throne set up in the place of the gods

8.pericope_label: Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not. Wherefore king Darius signed the writing and the decree
debates: How far the law of the Medes and Persians was really unalterable
What the king thought he was gaining by signing
Whether the decree was a rational law at all
outliers: Clarke rejects the common understanding of the unchangeable law, holding that no legislators could be so foolish and that only the due form of enactment is in view
Keil and Delitzsch answer a modern charge that the prohibition was a senseless law, arguing that it touched only religious petition and followed from the standing of the king
themes: A document carried in already written
A signature that cannot be taken back
A throne that gains a month of divinity
Laws changed at will until justice gives way to licence

10.pericope_label: Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime
debates: Whether the open window was necessary or reckless
Why prayer was made toward one city
Whether Daniel might have resisted the decree by other means
outliers: Ellicott has the prophet removing the lattices to see further toward Jerusalem, and reckons him close upon ninety years old at this point
Calvin turns the verse against those who would keep faith inwardly and drop its outward profession when the profession becomes dangerous
themes: A decree learned of too late to stop
A window that is not shut
A face turned toward a ruined temple
Watchers posted where the praying can be seen

11.pericope_label: Then these men assembled, and found Daniel praying and making supplication before his God. Then they came near, and spake before the king concerning the king’s decree; Hast thou not signed a decree, that every man that shall ask a petition of any God or man within thirty days, save of thee, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions
debates: Whether the trap could have been avoided
Why the accusers kept the name of Daniel back
What kind of place the den of lions was
outliers: Clarke asks what the den actually was and compares it to a royal menagerie kept for public amusement before deciding it was a place of execution
Keil and Delitzsch answer objections raised against the credibility of the account, that the watching is never described and that Daniel took no precaution
themes: A visit timed for the hour of prayer
A servant girl questioned at the door
A name kept out of the accusation on purpose
A king bound by his own signature

13.pericope_label: Then answered they and said before the king, That Daniel, which is of the children of the captivity of Judah, regardeth not thee, O king, nor the decree that thou hast signed, but maketh his petition three times a day. Then the king, when he heard these words, was sore displeased with himself
debates: Why the accusers named Daniel as a captive rather than an officer
Whether the king was displeased with himself or with Daniel
What the second assembling was meant to secure
outliers: Calvin sets Darius beside Pilate, a ruler who wished to release an innocent man and was mastered by the fear of what a faction would say
Clarke reconstructs the missing hours, with the king canvassing his lords one by one in private while the accusers gathered their own support
themes: A title chosen to make loyalty look like treason
A king going from one adviser to another as the sun goes down
Shame outweighing conscience
A crowd returning louder than it left

16.pericope_label: Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. Now the king spake and said unto Daniel, Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee. And a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords
debates: What the stone and the seals were for
Whether the parting word was a wish or a confidence
What kind of place the den was
outliers: Calvin turns the sealing into a providence, arranged so that unbroken seals would prove the deliverance no trick of men
Gill reports and dismisses as fabulous an old account that there were no stones in Babylon and that angels fetched this one from the land of Israel
themes: A king delivering up his own favourite
Seals set by men who trust nobody, least of all their king
A vaulted chamber whose shape nobody knows
A stone that shuts the rescuers out as well as in

18.pericope_label: Then the king went to his palace, and passed the night fasting: neither were instruments of musick brought before him: and his sleep went from him. Then the king arose very early in the morning, and went in haste unto the den of lions
debates: What was withheld from the king that night
Whether his grief amounted to repentance
What brought him to the den in person
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch abandon the rendering instruments of music for concubines, arguing the word from a cognate in another tongue
Gill reads the earnestness out of the writing itself, from a doubled word and a letter written larger than usual
themes: A palace with the music forbidden
An old man who cannot sleep for what he signed
Grief that stops short of undoing the wrong
A king running his own errand at first light

20.pericope_label: And when he came to the den, he cried with a lamentable voice unto Daniel: and the king spake and said to Daniel, O Daniel, servant of the living God, is thy God, whom thou servest continually, able to deliver thee from the lions? Then said Daniel unto the king, O king, live for ever
debates: Whether the question shows faith or doubt
Whether Darius was converted by any of this
Why Daniel made no complaint of the king
outliers: Ellicott tracks the faith of the king across the chapter as a rising and falling thing, weaker here than when he passed sentence and stronger later than that of an earlier king
Calvin denies that the confession proves any conversion, holding that the king only added the God of Israel to the idols he already kept
themes: A cry more like howling than speech
A pagan mouth using a name it does not own
A question that doubts what cannot be doubted
An injured man who says only, live for ever

22.pericope_label: My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions’ mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me; and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt. Then was the king exceeding glad for him, and commanded that they should take Daniel up out of the den
debates: Which angel was sent
What the claim of innocence before the king amounts to
What it means that he believed in his God
outliers: Calvin turns aside to the men who fight for good causes and fail, tracing their ruin to self-confidence and ambition, and quoting the saying of Brutus that virtue is a frivolous thing
Clarke answers the question of why no hurt was found with a catalogue of everything faith is said to accomplish
themes: A den turned into a lodging by one presence
Beasts held on an invisible leash
An offence against a law that was no offence against the king
Not a scratch found on a body left among lions

24.pericope_label: And the king commanded, and they brought those men which had accused Daniel, and they cast them into the den of lions, them, their children, and their wives; and the lions had the mastery of them. Then king Darius wrote unto all people, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth; Peace be multiplied unto you
debates: Whether the punishment of the families was just
Whether the edict shows any real change in the king
How far the address to all the earth reaches
outliers: Clarke accepts the justice of the sentence on the accusers and calls the killing of their wives and children savage cruelty
Calvin argues from the speed of the lions, which devoured a whole crowd as it fell, that their restraint the night before can have been nothing natural
themes: Beasts that do not wait for their prey to land
An edict that goes further than the last and still not far enough
A god given the highest place among gods
Every dominion of one kingdom mistaken for the world

26.pericope_label: I make a decree, That in every dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel: for he is the living God, and stedfast for ever, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed. He delivereth and rescueth, and he worketh signs and wonders in heaven and in earth. So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian
debates: Whether the decree amounts to a confession of the true God
What the end of his dominion means
What the closing notice settles about the two reigns
outliers: Ellicott attributes the Scriptural cast of the decree to Daniel having had a hand in drafting it, and takes the end named in it for the close of all heathen kingdoms
Calvin allows that the king reasons correctly from the one deliverance and still denies him the substance of the confession, since he knows nothing of why God delivers his own
themes: A decree that reverses one signed a month earlier
A list of divine titles in a pagan hand
A courtier who outlived five masters
A prophet obscure under one crown and honoured under the next
